# About Glenmore

Dear all,

I have some news about the house in Glenmore, and I want you to hear the whole of it from me.

I have agreed to sell it. The sale was agreed on 3 November, and it is due to close on **15 January 2027**. I should have told everyone myself before the news got around, and I am sorry for how some of you found out. I don’t want the date, or anything else about it, coming to you second-hand again.

The house has been part of this family for a long time. Pádraig Mulkerrin, Tom’s grandfather, built it in 1931, near Oughterard. It was where Tom grew up, and it has held a great many of our days since. I know it means different things to each of you, and I know this news will not be easy for everyone. It hasn’t been easy for me either.

I also want to say straight away that I’m inviting everyone who can make it to a family day at the house on **Sunday 13 December**, before it is cleared. We’ll have soup and sandwiches. Bring wellies. There will be plenty of time to go through the rooms, walk around outside and be there together. I know Boston and Perth are a long way to come, and Leeds isn’t exactly up the road either, so I’ll understand if you can’t be there. But the invitation is for all of you.

Since Tom died in March 2024, I’ve been driving out to Glenmore every fortnight to air the house and check the pipes. It’s forty minutes each way. At first, going out there was something I needed to do, as well as something the house needed. I could open the door, get the air through the rooms and make sure everything was all right. It gave me a reason to keep going back.

But I need to tell you something I haven’t told anyone until now. Last February, there was frost on the step at the back door and I slipped. I lay there for twenty minutes before I could get up. I told nobody, and I know I should have. The truth is that since then I have been afraid of being alone at the house. I still went out, because the house needed looking after, but I was afraid of falling again with nobody there.

That fall isn’t the only reason for the sale, but it is part of it, and I don’t want to leave it out now. I am not able to go on maintaining the house. The drive, the checking and the work it needs have become too much for me.

In September, Ó Flaithearta’s did a roof survey. There are slates to be dealt with and work needed on the back chimney, and the quote came to €38,000. There is also the damp in the back bedroom. The septic tank needs replacing to sell the house to anyone anyway. These are not small jobs, and they are not things I can keep putting off.

I’ve thought about all of this over the best part of two years. I know the house is more than a list of repairs. If it were only a matter of a roof and a tank, this would be a much shorter post. But the repairs are real, and so is the fact that I can’t manage the place as it needs to be managed.

The couple buying it are Aoife and Kevin Joyce. Kevin is from Maam Cross, and they have two small children. They want to live in the house; they are not buying it as a holiday let. They offered a fair price. It was less than the Dublin crowd offered during the summer, and I took the lower offer on purpose. It matters to me that there will be a family living there.

Tom used to say that the house should have children in it, not be a museum. I’ve thought about that often. I can imagine him saying it plainly, and then getting on with whatever else he was doing. I don’t mean that the decision was his to make, or that I can use his words to settle how anyone else feels. It is my decision. But I’m glad that, if the sale goes through, there will be children making their own memories there.

Some things are staying with us. The dresser is going to Úna’s, and I’m keeping Pádraig’s fiddle, the photographs, the Sacred Heart lamp and the gate sign. We’ll have those things in the family.

Aoife and Kevin have also said that the family can come out and walk the land any time. I’m grateful to them for that. I know it won’t be the same as having the house in the family, and I’m not going to pretend it will be. But it means a great deal that they have offered.

There are things I can see in my mind as clearly as if they happened yesterday. Tom proposed to me in the haggard behind the house in 1979. It was raining, and the cattle were watching us. I don’t remember thinking at the time that we were making a story the family would hear for years afterwards. I was too busy saying yes.

And I remember the children learning to swim in the lake below the house. Declan would refuse to come out until his lips were blue. We could call and call, and there he’d be, still in the water. I hope some of you remember those days too.

Declan, I want to speak to you here, because I know you read the blog. You heard about the sale from your cousin Gráinne on WhatsApp, not from me. You rang me at two in the morning your time and said I was “selling Dad”. I said things back that I shouldn’t have, and I’m sorry for those things.

I regret that I didn’t consult you. You should have heard from me, and you should have had the chance to talk to me before it reached you the way it did. I understand that the house is tied up with your dad and that this hurts. I can’t undo the way you found out, though I wish I could.

I also need to be honest that I’m not willing to wait until your summer visit. I know you wanted that time, but I have come to the point where I need to do this now. I’m sorry for how I handled telling you; I’m not sorry for making the decision.

I’m not angry with you, Declan. My door is open, and I hope we can talk. You don’t have to agree with me for that to happen.

For everyone else, I know there may be questions, and perhaps some of you are cross with me too. You’re entitled to feel as you do. I should have spoken to the family properly instead of leaving room for the news to go around in bits on the phone. I’m sorry for that.

Over the best part of these two years, I’ve come to realise that I can keep Tom’s memory without keeping the house. It has taken me time to say that, and saying it doesn’t make it any less sad to leave Glenmore. I will miss knowing that the door is ours to open. I will miss the place where he grew up, where he proposed to me, and where our children spent those days at the lake.

But I have those memories, and so do you. The Joyces will have a home, and we will still have the stories and the things we’re keeping. I hope that, on 13 December, we can spend a day at the house together before it is cleared. We can have our soup and sandwiches, put on our wellies and take the time to say goodbye to it in our own ways.

With love to you all.
